title: Embrace the Reality Monster
body: **The problem with both sides of the passion debate**
Follow your passion or be realistic and chase the money. Both are wrong, for the same reason: neither one is actually about reality. They're feelings dressed up as strategy.
The truth: people pay for value. Not for how much you love something. For what it does for them. If your passion doesn't make someone else's life better, the market doesn't care how obsessed you are.

But skip the obsession and chase the money instead, and you hit a different wall. Faked motivation runs out. Most worthwhile outcomes take years, and you can't fake obsession for years. The people who outlast everyone else aren't the ones who wanted the payout most, they're the ones who couldn't have stopped if they tried.

Some constraints don't move. What the market values, what compounds, what people actually pay for, these are closer to physics than opinion. Fight them and you just burn energy against something that was never going to bend. Find the overlap, where what you're obsessed with meets what people will actually pay for.
**The part of reality that looks like defiance**

Some of the most successful people got there by believing something that wasn't true yet. Not confidence, near delusion. That irrational belief is what let them survive the years the market said stop. They kept failing and adjusting and never quit, not because the data told them to keep going, but because they'd already decided they would.

It looks like defiance, but it's actually the opposite. Persistence and self-belief are part of reality too. Most people quit right before the inflection point, and the ones who don't disproportionately win. So irrational self-belief isn't fighting reality, it's using one of its real mechanisms: conviction changes what you'll attempt, and attempts compound.
**Why the cold rational model is wrong**

Understanding reality isn't about becoming a cold calculator who only does the provably smart thing. That leaves out one of reality's real forces: belief is causal. It changes what you try, what you endure, what you become capable of.

The people who look most realistic, grinding, persisting, believing something the data hasn't caught up to, often understand reality best. They've just sorted which laws are immovable and which only look that way until someone refuses to accept it.
That sorting is the actual skill. Not passive acceptance, but learning reality's shape, obeying what doesn't move, and bending what does by sheer will.
